title: Guha the boatman
hook: a boat on the Ganga, Sita's prayer in midstream, and a famous boatman who isn't in Valmiki

segments.voice: Yesterday: jata, matted hair at dawn, after a night when two men shared one grief. Today, across the river.

If you've heard this part of the story at a temple or a family reading, you may remember a boatman who won't let Rama into his boat until he's washed his feet. He's afraid, he says with a grin, that the dust of those feet will turn his wooden boat into a woman, the way it once turned a stone into Ahalya. It's a lovely, funny scene. It comes from a later retelling, Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas. Valmiki's crossing is simpler, with its own quiet center.
screen: `WASH YOUR FEET FIRST.` → `A STORY FROM TULSIDAS.` → `VALMIKI'S CROSSING IS SIMPLER.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki, Guha arranges everything. He has a strong, well-made boat brought down to the bank, with oarsmen ready. Rama thanks him and says goodbye. Sita steps in first, then Lakshmana, then Rama, and the oarsmen push off into the current. In midstream, Sita folds her hands and speaks to the river itself, to Ganga, as a goddess. She asks Ganga to protect Rama through the fourteen years and bring the three of them back safely, and she vows to worship the river with offerings when they return. We won't repeat the prayer here, but its shape matters: the first time the exiles leave dry land, Sita turns the crossing into worship. In Hindu tradition, the Ganga is still this: a goddess and a mother as well as a river, someone you can speak to. The boat reaches the far bank, and they're truly outside the kingdom. Rama sets an order for walking: Lakshmana first, to clear the way, Sita in the middle, Rama last, guarding them both. Guha watches from the far shore until they're gone among the trees. So Valmiki's boatman isn't the comic figure of the later story. He's a king, a friend, a host who kept watch all night and provided the boat. Two retellings, two boatmen. Valmiki's is the one who stays on the bank, watching.
screen: `GUHA BRINGS A STRONG BOAT.` · `SITA SPEAKS TO THE RIVER.` · `THE GANGA, GODDESS AND MOTHER.` · `LAKSHMANA AHEAD, RAMA BEHIND.` · then, large: `GUHA WATCHES FROM THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: Imagine a small boat in the middle of a wide river, rising a little on each breath in and settling on each breath out. You're between two shores, what you're leaving and what's ahead; don't hurry toward either. If you pray, you can ask for safe passage, in your own way.
Ganga, the river honored as a goddess and a mother. Guha sees the exiles across her, Sita prays to her in midstream, and Guha watches them disappear into the forest.
Your line: Guha watches from the shore. Ahead, a sage where two rivers meet. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindu pilgrims bathe in the Ganga, offer lamps and flowers to it, and speak to it as Ganga Ma, a mother goddess; in the text, Sita prays to the river in midstream.

original.note: Sanskrit gaṅgā: the river Ganga, honored as a goddess and a mother; the river the exiles cross today.

trapdoor: what you thought: the boatman who ferried Rama is a humble ferryman.
what it means: in Valmiki, it's Guha, a king and Rama's friend, who provides the boat.
what a scholar hears: the foot-washing boatman, often called Kevat, comes from the Ramcharitmanas, one of the places where Tulsidas adds a devotional scene to Valmiki's frame.

chat.says: Why did Sita talk to the river while they were crossing it?
options: In Hindu tradition the Ganga is a goddess and mother; Sita prayed for a safe return.
She was frightened of the strong current and was calling back to Guha for help.
She was saying goodbye to Ayodhya, since the river flows right past the city.
chat.meaning: Sita speaks to Ganga as a goddess, asking protection for Rama and a safe return, and vows offerings when they come home.
